In this question you must show all stages of your working. Solutions relying entirely on calculator technology are not acceptable.

$\mathrm{f}(x) = 4x^3 + 5x^2 - 10x + 4a$, $x \in \mathbb{R}$, where $a$ is a positive constant.

Given $(x - a)$ is a factor of $\mathrm{f}(x)$,
(a) show that
$a(4a^2 + 5a - 6) = 0$ (2)
(b) Hence
 (i) find the value of $a$
 (ii) use algebra to find the exact solutions of the equation
$\mathrm{f}(x) = 3$ (4)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Attempts $\mathrm{f}(a) = 0$, leading to an equation in $a$ only, and attempts to take a factor of $a$ out (condone slips; the "$=0$" may appear on a later line, but must be seen at some point in the solution). A1*: Achieves $a(4a^2+5a-6) = 0$ with no errors, including brackets (minimum acceptable is $4a^3+5a^2-10a+4a=0 \Rightarrow a(4a^2+5a-6)=0$; given answer, so working must be fully shown, and simply finding $a$ and substituting it into $\mathrm{f}(x)$ does not score). (2 marks)
(b)(i) B1: Deduces that $a = \frac{3}{4}$ only (may be implied by their resultant cubic); if (b)(ii) is repeated using other roots for which $a \neq \frac{3}{4}$, those solutions must be rejected. (ii) M1: Attempts to substitute $a = \frac{3}{4}$ (which must be positive) into $\mathrm{f}(x)$, sets $\mathrm{f}(x) = 3$ and collects terms on one side ($=0$ may be implied); condone arithmetical/sign slips. B1: $x = 0$ is a solution. A1: $x = \frac{-5 \pm \sqrt{185}}{8}$ (and these values only), or exact equivalent (ignore $0$ for this mark); this mark cannot be scored if they proceed directly to the roots from $4x^3+5x^2-10x$ without taking a factor of, or dividing by, $x$ first to see the quadratic factor; withhold if the fraction line was clearly not intended to cover both terms. (4 marks)

Relative to a fixed origin $O$,
• the point $A$ has position vector $5\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j} + 2\mathbf{k}$
• the point $B$ has position vector $2\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j} + a\mathbf{k}$
where $a$ is a positive integer.
(a) Show that $|\overrightarrow{OA}| = \sqrt{38}$ (1)
(b) Find the smallest value of $a$ for which
$|\overrightarrow{OB}| > |\overrightarrow{OA}|$ (2)

The curve $C$ has equation $y = \mathrm{f}(x)$ where $x \in \mathbb{R}$

questions.question_text:
Given that
$a = \log_2 x$
$b = \log_2(x + 8)$
Express in terms of $a$ and/or $b$
(a) $\log_2 \sqrt{x}$ (1)
(b) $\log_2(x^2 + 8x)$ (2)
(c) $\log_2\left(8 + \frac{64}{x}\right)$
 Give your answer in simplest form. (3)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
Condone omission of base 2 throughout.
(a) B1: $\frac{a}{2}$, or $0.5a$, isw. (1 mark)
(b) M1: Takes a factor of $x$ out of the bracket to achieve $\log_2[x(x+8)]$ and attempts to apply the addition law of logs, usually leading to $\log_2 x + \log_2(x+8)$ (condone missing brackets or omission of base 2; may be implied by a correct answer; allow if they write $\log_2 x + \log_2 x + \log_2 8$, an answer of $2a+3$ scores M1A0). A1: $a+b$, or simplified equivalent (isw). (2 marks)
(c) B1: Writes $8 + \frac{64}{x}$ as a single fraction, e.g. $\frac{8x+64}{x}$ or $\frac{8(x+8)}{x}$ or $8x^{-1}(x+8)$ (may be implied by later work e.g. $\log_2 8 - \log_2 x + \log_2(x+8)$). M1: Attempts to apply the laws of logs, uses $\log_2 8 = 3$ and proceeds to $3 \pm \log_2 x \pm \log_2(x+8)$ (may be implied by $3 \pm b \pm a$; condone invisible brackets around $x+8$ and omission of base 2; note $\log_2(x+8)$ written as $\log_2 x + \log_2 8$ is M0). A1: $3+b-a$, or simplified equivalent (isw). (3 marks)

A circle $C$ has equation
$x^2 + y^2 + 6kx - 2ky + 7 = 0$
where $k$ is a constant.
(a) Find in terms of $k$,

(b) Find the range of possible values of $k$. (6)

questions.question_text:
The value, $V$ pounds, of a mobile phone, $t$ months after it was bought, is modelled by
$V = ab^t$
where $a$ and $b$ are constants.
Figure 2 shows the linear relationship between $\log_{10} V$ and $t$.
The line passes through the points $(0, 3)$ and $(10, 2.79)$ as shown.
Using these points,
(a) find the initial value of the phone, (2)
(b) find a complete equation for $V$ in terms of $t$, giving the exact value of $a$ and giving the value of $b$ to 3 significant figures. (3)
Exactly 2 years after it was bought, the value of the phone was £$320$
(c) Use this information to evaluate the reliability of the model. (2)

(a) M1: Sets $\log_{10} V = 3$ and attempts to find a value for $a$, or an expression for $V$ when $t=0$, scoring for sight of $10^3$ or the correct answer implied (there may be more complicated routes, e.g. finding the complete equation $\log_{10} V = 3 + \left[\frac{2.79-3}{10}\right]t$ first, then setting $\log_{10} V=3 \Rightarrow V=10^3$). A1: $V = £1000$ cao (including units; do not accept $£10^3$). (2 marks)
(b) Mark (b) and (c) together - note that work seen in (a) must be used in (b) to score. M1: Either finds the gradient between the two points, e.g. $\frac{2.79-3}{10-0} = -0.021$ (do not condone sign slips; may be implied by sight of $10^{-0.021}$), or finds the equation $\log_{10} V = 3 - \text{"}0.021\text{"}t$ (may be unsimplified). M1: Attempts to find the value or an expression for $b$ using their gradient or equation, e.g. scores for the expression $10^{\text{"}-0.021\text{"}}$ oe, or by equating coefficients from $\log_{10} V = \log_{10} a + (\log_{10} b)t$, or by using $10^{2.79} = \text{"}1000\text{"}b^{10}$ and proceeding to e.g. $b=\sqrt[10]{\text{"}0.61659\ldots\text{"}}$. questions.question_text:
Prove, using algebra, that
$(n + 1)^3 - n^3$
is odd for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}^+$ (4)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
General guidance: a mixture of methods/approaches is likely; mark the approach scoring the highest number of marks. There should be no errors in the algebra, but allow e.g. invisible brackets to be "recovered". Withhold the final mark if $n$ is used instead of $k$, or if the conclusion refers to $n \in \mathbb{R}$ ($n \in \mathbb{Z}^+$ is acceptable).
Main scheme (algebraic method using $n=2k$ and $n=2k \pm 1$) - you will need to look at both cases (odd and even $n$) and mark the one which is fully correct first.
M1: For the key step, attempts to find $(n+1)^3-n^3$ when $n=2k$ or $n=2k \pm 1$, and attempts to multiply out and simplify to a three-term quadratic (allow equivalent representations of odd/even, e.g. $n=2k+2$ or $2n \pm 5$; condone arithmetical slips and condone the use of e.g. $n=2n$ and $n=2n \pm 1$). A1: A complete argument for $n=2k$ or $n=2k+1$ (or $n=2k-1$) showing the result is odd, requiring: a correct simplified quadratic expression (e.g. $12k^2+6k+1$ when $n=2k$, $12k^2+18k+7$ when $n=2k+1$, $12k^2-6k+1$ when $n=2k-1$; may be factorised), a reason why the expression is odd (e.g. writing it as $2k(6k+3)+1$, or via a divisibility argument), and a "hence odd" conclusion for that case. dM1: Attempts to find $(n+1)^3-n^3$ for both $n=2k$ and $n=2k+1$ (or $n=2k-1$) and attempts to multiply out and simplify each to a three-term quadratic (dependent on the previous method mark; condone the same slips as above). A1*: A complete argument for both $n=2k$ and $n=2k+1$ (or $n=2k-1$), requiring for both cases: correct simplified expressions (which may be factorised), a reason why each is odd, a minimal conclusion for each (which may be within the overall final conclusion), and an overall concluding statement covering all $n$, e.g. "Hence odd for all $n(\in \mathbb{Z}^+)$" (accept "hence proven", "statement proved", "QED") - given answer, so working must be fully shown for both cases. (4 marks)
Alternative valid methods seen include: an algebraic-with-logic method (multiplying out to $3n^2+3n+1$, factorising as $3n(n+1)+1$, and arguing $n(n+1)$ is always even as the product of two consecutive integers, so $3n(n+1)+1$ is odd); a proof-by-contradiction method (setting $3n^2+3n+1=2k$ for some integer $k$, rearranging to $3n(n+1)=2k-1$, and reaching a contradiction since $3n(n+1)$ must be even); a pure-logic method considering odd/even $n$ separately with no algebraic manipulation (scores a maximum of SC 1010 if fully correct); and (Further Maths) a proof by induction. Each alternative scores by the same M1A1dM1A1* mark allocation applied to its own equivalent milestones [editor: (see full mark scheme notes for exact wording of each)].
